title: Off-Plan Buyers Check Your Past. What Will They Find?
seoTitle: Off-Plan Buyers Check Your Past: What Will They Find?
description: Buyers compare your old launch renderings with Google Street View today. Why your last building sells your next project, and how to use that proof first.
answer: In about an hour on their phone, buyers find a developer's old projects, pull up the launch renderings and compare them with Google Street View today. A big gap makes them doubt your new project. A small gap is your best marketing, so show that comparison before they look.
body:
Your buyers have a free tool on their phone that, in one hour, tells them more about you than your entire sales gallery. Most developers have no idea buyers are using it.

## Buyers check the story now

In a previous episode I described the **verification gap**: the distance between what a developer promised and what they built. This time, the developer's side.

Buyers no longer just listen to your story. They check it. They need no lawyer and no inspector, just an hour online, and with AI tools that research is faster and deeper than ever.

## What they actually do

1. **They look at your past, not your present.** Your projects from five, seven, ten years ago are the only real evidence of what you deliver.
2. **They open Google Maps and switch to Street View** at those addresses. Facade, landscaping, finishes, the amenities you promised, the surroundings.
3. **They find your old marketing.** Renderings, walkthroughs, videos and brochures from those launches are still online.
4. **They put the two side by side.**

## The burger test

Everyone has done this with food. On the menu the burger is tall and perfect, cheese melting, bun shining. The one in the box looks like someone sat on it. You eat it, but you never trust that menu again.

Now imagine the burger cost two, three or five million dollars. That is what happens when buyers compare your old renderings with your finished building. If the gap is big, they do not just doubt the old project. They doubt the new one you are presenting.

**Your next project is not sold by your next rendering. It is sold by your last building.** Every project you deliver is evidence for you or against you.

## If your gap is small, use it

Here is the good news. If you delivered buildings that look like their renderings, with the amenities and the timeline you promised, that is the best marketing asset you have, and almost nobody uses it. It sits on a portfolio page nobody reads.

Do what your buyers will do anyway, before they do it:

- Put old renderings next to photos of the finished buildings.
- Show launch dates and delivery dates.
- List the amenities promised and the amenities delivered.

When buyers find the proof themselves, it feels like an investigation. When you show it first, it feels like confidence.

## Then give data for the current project

Go one step further on the project you are selling now. Give buyers data, not just dreams: the floorplan of their unit, the real dimensions, the orientation, the view from every window, the finishes. Let them walk through every unit, not just the hero unit.

When a developer gives little data and a lot of dream, buyers wonder what is missing. When a developer gives the data openly, buyers conclude something simple: this developer is not afraid of the truth.

Your buyers will check your past. The only question is whether they find a gap on their own, or proof you showed them first.
takeaways: Buyers compare your old launch renderings with Google Street View in about an hour.
A big gap between promise and delivery makes buyers doubt your new project.
Your last building sells your next project more than any new rendering.
If your record is good, show the side-by-side proof before buyers look for it.
For the current project, give unit-level data so your vision is believable.
faq: How do buyers research an off-plan developer?
They find the developer's older projects, look them up in Google Street View, find the original launch renderings online and compare the two.
What is the verification gap in real estate?
The difference between what a developer promised at launch and what they actually built and delivered.
How can developers use their track record in marketing?
By showing launch renderings next to photos of the finished buildings, with promised and actual delivery dates and amenities.
